questions.question: Why is if err != nil the standard Go error check?
questions.title: Is If Err != Nil The Standard
questions.direct_answer: Errors are values: functions return (result, error); the caller checks immediately at the point of failure. The if err != nil block IS Go's exception handling.

Mental Model

```mermaid

    NILVAR[nil channel] --> SENDS[send: parks forever]
    NILVAR --> RECV[receive: parks forever]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The pattern is the visible half of a design decision. The invisible half: what Go got rid of. Exception systems interleave two control flows — normal and exceptional — and every call site is secretly a branch point whether it looks like one or not. Go's answer removes the second control flow from the language: errors ride returns, so there's exactly one flow to read.

The compound effect of small rules: multi-return makes the pair expressible; unused-variable checking means you can't grab the value while ignoring the error slot without WRITING your ignoring (_ is explicit); no finally/catch means the handling is inline, where the failure happened.

What reviewers actually do with this: read failure paths as first-class code. In a catch-based system, the handler is a paragraph elsewhere describing hypothetical failures; in Go, the handler is adjacent to the operation that can fail, with the state it needs (which file, which step) still in scope. Reviewers can see that os.ReadFile's failure is handled by wrapping with the path — because the path variable is right there.

The honest cost accounting, because interviews reward it: the verbosity is real, error wrapping is manual discipline (nothing forces %w over %v), and the check-shape repeats without abstraction. Go's position is that these costs buy total auditability — every failure path is in the diff. Whether that trade wins is the actual debate; knowing both sides is the answer.

questions.question: Should you check err after checking the result?
questions.title: Should You Check Err After Checking The
questions.direct_answer: Check err first. On failure, other returns are zero values — reading them before the check is the classic bug.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of If Err Not Nil Pattern.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Check err first.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Check the error before anything else. The convention — on failure, other return values are zero/nil — means reading the result before the check reads garbage:

```go
n, err := reader.Read(buf)
process(buf[:n])   // BUG on error: n is 0, or worse, stale
if err != nil {
    return err
}
```

The order matters because the zero-value convention makes the result slot meaningless when err is non-nil. buf[:0] processes nothing — silently, no error — or with a partially-filled buffer from a previous call, processes stale data. Either way the bug is invisible until you trace why 'nothing happened.'

The guard-first shape:

```go
n, err := reader.Read(buf)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
process(buf[:n])   // n is valid ONLY below the guard
```

The one documented exception: io.Reader's Read returns the count of bytes read before an error (including io.EOF) — data read before the failure is real, and callers should use it. That exception is famous BECAUSE it's the exception: everywhere else, the rule is absolute — err first, values after, never reversed.

```mermaid
    CHK -->|yes| RET[return / handle / wrap with %w]
    CHK -->|no| USE[v is valid here]
    RET --> NEXT[next frame repeats the pattern]
```

questions.question: What is the difference between returning err and wrapping it?
questions.title: Is Checking Err == Nil Instead Of
questions.direct_answer: Returning err passes it up unchanged; fmt.Errorf with %w adds context while keeping errors.Is/As working. Wrap when you add meaning; pass through when you add nothing.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of If Err Not Nil Pattern.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Returning err passes it up unchanged; fmt.Errorf with %w adds context while keeping errors.Is/As working.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    B[base error] --> W1[fmt.Errorf %w — chain edge]
    W1 --> W2[another %w wrap — context added]
    W2 --> IS[errors.Is walks the chain — finds base]
    W1 --> AS[errors.As extracts types through it]
    V[%v instead] --> CUT[chain severed — Is fails]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The choice is really about WHERE the reader's attention lands when something fails. A returned error's message chain reads top-down: the outermost wrap is the operation the caller attempted; each inner layer adds the context that layer had. That narrative structure is why wrapping with the right local facts is the default:

```go
// reads: 'start server: listen :8080: address already in use'
return fmt.Errorf("start server: %w", err)
```
versus passing raw, where the caller sees only 'address already in use' with no hint of what was being attempted. Same failure, different debugging cost.

The over-wrap anti-pattern has a signature: wrap messages that are pure ceremony. 'failed:', 'error:', 'operation failed:' add zero facts and the stack reads 'failed: failed: failed: address already in use' — the reader strips them mentally. The test: if your wrap text isn't a noun phrase or a fact (a file name, an operation, a step), it doesn't earn the line.

%w vs %v in the wrap is the other half of the discipline: %w preserves the chain so callers can Is/As; %v prints the same text but amputates the inspectability. Since no tooling warns %v-that-should-be-%w, it's convention — write %w by default, and reserve %v for terminal human-only formatting at the top of the program where no code will inspect below.

questions.question: What is the blank identifier's role with errors?
questions.title: Ifference Between Returning Err And Wrapping It
questions.direct_answer: _, err := f() keeps only the error. v, _ := f() discards the error — a lint smell unless failure is genuinely impossible. _ makes ignoring an explicit choice.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of If Err Not Nil Pattern.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: _, err := f() keeps only the error. v, _ := f() discards the error — a lint smell unless failure is genuinely impossible.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The blank identifier is Go's escape valve for unused returns, and errors are where it matters most:

```go
_, err := f()    // need only the error — fine, common
v, _ := f()      // take the value, ignore the error — the dangerous one
```

`v, _` is legal Go and sometimes correct — best-effort writes, metrics, caches where failure changes nothing. The _ documents the decision at the call site: a reader sees the error was considered and dropped, not overlooked.

But most `v, _` in real code is a latent bug. The failure doesn't vanish — it moves downstream. The zero value gets used, and the cause becomes 'why is this empty?' three weeks later. No compile error, no test failure — the error was already gone at the point where it could have been handled.

That's why errcheck exists as a linter: the language permits discarding, the ecosystem flags it. The alternatives in order of effort: log it (`v, err := f(); if err != nil { log... }` — three lines, failure becomes diagnosable), handle it, or propagate it. Reach for `_` only when you can say why the error doesn't matter — out loud, at that line.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Q[the question] --> R[the core rule]
    R --> EX[the small example]
    EX --> B[the boundary — where the rule ends]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
_ is the only way to opt out of a return value in Go, and its error-slot usage divides into three patterns of very different health:

1. `_, err := f()` — want the error only. Common and correct: existence checks, did-it-succeed calls. Nothing lost.

2. `v, _ := f()` — want the value only. The dangerous one. The error is gone at the moment it occurred; the zero value flows onward. The failure isn't handled — it's POSTPONED, to wherever the zero value misbehaves. That indirection is what makes these bugs hard: the crash site is three functions away from the cause site.

3. A bare `f()` — only legal when f returns nothing. When f returns an error, the call alone doesn't compile — Go requires the assignment shape for multi-return, which is precisely why _ exists: the language makes ignoring a DECISION — you type it.

That's the design insight: languages without this forcing function let failures disappear silently (unchecked exceptions, ignored return codes via lint-only warnings). Go makes ignore an explicit token at the exact line — so code review can catch it, linters can flag it, and the reader can ask 'why?'. The errcheck linter exists because reviewers asked it enough. The rule that survives review: every _ on an error slot carries a justifying comment — or it doesn't survive.

questions.question: Why does Go not use try/catch?
questions.title: Es Go Not Use Try/catch
questions.direct_answer: Visible failure paths: signatures document what can fail, callers deal at the call site, and the compiler enforces acknowledgment. Panic is reserved for program bugs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of If Err Not Nil Pattern.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Visible failure paths: signatures document what can fail, callers deal at the call site, and the compiler enforces acknowledgment.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Go's designers looked at exception systems and saw a cost they didn't want: invisible control flow. Any call in an exception language might throw — the failure path isn't in the code, it's in the documentation. Go made the opposite trade: failure is a value in the signature, and the caller must acknowledge it before using the result.

What that buys:

Auditable failure — reading a function shows its failure handling; there is no elsewhere to check.

Forced acknowledgment — unused-variable rules mean you can't silently skip the error; discarding it requires writing _, which is a visible choice.

Local reasoning — the failure and its handling are adjacent, in the same function, at the same call. No unwinding through five frames to find the handler.

What it costs: the ceremony is real. Three lines per fallible call, in every layer, forever. The Go community's own essays acknowledge this — the verbosity is the price of the visibility, and the bet is that visibility wins at maintenance time.

The design keeps panic/recover for the other kind of failure — the program is wrong, not the input — which is why the two mechanisms don't overlap: try/catch conflates expected failure with bugs; Go splits them at the language level.

```go
// the entire mechanism:
v, err := doWork()
if err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("context: %w", err)  // visible, wrap, propagate
}
// v valid here — no catch, no throw, the check IS the handling
```

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[symptom] --> E[evidence]
    E --> C[cause]
    C --> F[fix]
    F --> T[the test that proves it]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The historical answer is specific: Go's designers (Pike, Thompson, Griesemer — all with deep Unix/C lineage) watched 20 years of C++/Java exception practice and concluded the cost wasn't the syntax, it was the semantics: exceptions make failure paths invisible and composition unpredictable.

The invisible-path problem: any call might throw anything. API surfaces can't say what fails; docs must. Callers can't locally reason; they must know the exception graph. Java's 'catch or declare' was the strongest enforcement ever tried — and it still left RuntimeException as the un-declared back door.

The unpredictable-composition problem: handlers interact with scope and cleanup in ways that make refactoring hazardous — moving a call across a try boundary changes which handler sees it, and destructors/finally interleave with unwinding in orders that surprise even experts.

Go's replacement is deliberately boring: errors ride return values, so the type system carries the failure surface, callers read it from the signature, and cleanup rides defer (which composes linearly — LIFO at scope exit, no unwinding interleaving). The result: every function is a contract you can read in one line. The cost — verbosity — was priced in consciously.

For interviews: acknowledge the trade honestly. 'Go chose visible ceremony over invisible control flow' is fair to both sides. The strongest counterpoint is Java's checked exceptions' unpopularity; the strongest rebuttal is Go's own error-wrapping evolution (errors.Is/As and %w were added BECAUSE bare returned errors were too weak for composition) — the design iterates toward usability while keeping the visibility.
